annotation.p: Cartographer Lida Rakitina arrives at a lighthouse on the White Sea, soon to be automated, to sort through the papers of her late grandfather, a hydrographer. Among the waterlogged logbooks she finds a chart with one mark too many: a seventh light, absent from every official register.

Her search for the missing signal leads Lida to Sukhoy Kamen, an old shipping incident, and a man whose name no one has dared speak aloud for years. When the island loses all contact with the outside world and a launch enters the wrong channel, the secret of the past becomes the only way to bring its people home.
The Seventh Light is an original novella of the North, about memory, precision, and charts that do more than show the way: they carry a responsibility for it.

author.nickname: The Turn the Page Editorial Team

epigraph.p: A shoreline cannot be drawn once and for all.
The sea corrects the drawing twice a day.
epigraph.text-author: From a manual for northern cartographers

section.p: The envelope lay on the drawing table, on top of a chart of the White Sea, as though its sender had chosen the right place for it beforehand. There was no return address, only Lida Rakitina’s name and four numbers separated by dots. Rain had blurred the postmark. The paper smelled of damp wood and machine oil—the smell of the crates of field logbooks delivered to the Northern Hydrographic Bureau.

Lida copied the numbers onto tracing paper, though she knew them by heart. The sixty-sixth parallel, Tonky Island, Cape Krestovy. That was where the lighthouse stood, where her grandfather Semyon Rakitin had served as the last civilian hydrographer. Nine years had passed since his death. In that time Lida had graduated, learned not to confuse precision with certainty, and refused three times to sort through his papers.

Inside the envelope was half a page from the watch log. Its blue squares had bled along the fold, but her grandfather’s handwriting was still unmistakable: he kept his figures upright and drew the Cyrillic letter ‘д’ downwards, as if dropping an anchor. Beneath the tide table was a single sentence: “If the sixth goes out, look for the seventh somewhere other than the shore.” No signature, no explanation.

Enclosed with the letter were a ticket for the motor vessel Onega and an official assignment. The bureau was sending Lida to Tonky to inventory the lighthouse archive. In a month the light was to be switched to automatic control, the keeper’s house mothballed, and the old logbooks digitised or discarded. At the bottom were the director’s signature and a pencilled note from the secretary: “You asked for fieldwork yourself.”

She had, indeed. She was tired of straight walls, satellite images, and shorelines she could correct on a screen with a keystroke. But Tonky Island was more than fieldwork. As a child, Lida had spent her Augusts there, counting the steps of the spiral staircase and falling asleep to the slow beat of the lens turning above her ceiling. Then came the accident off Sukhoy Kamen. Her grandfather was removed from his post, the family stopped going north, and the grown-ups learned to break off a conversation at the word “lighthouse”.

Lida took out an old nautical chart. On it, Cape Krestovy resembled a cupped hand. Six navigational lights were marked around it: two harbour lights, three leading lights1, and the main lighthouse. There was no seventh.

Eighteen hours remained before the Onega sailed. Lida switched off the lamp above the table, but the envelope did not disappear into the dark. It glowed white on the blue chart, a little window. She slipped her dividers, a waterproof notebook, and her grandfather’s magnifying glass into her rucksack; for years the glass had lain in her bottom drawer. By morning the decision felt less like a decision than a journey already begun.

The motor vessel sailed north for a day. At first low shores slipped past the saloon windows; then the water grew grey and wide. The passengers spoke more softly than they had at the terminal, as if the sea demanded a different voice. Lida sat by the glass, reading a copy of the accident file. In the official entry it all looked simple: on the night of 22–23 October, Senior Hydrographer Rakitin had permitted an unregistered signal to be lit, causing the tug Toros to deviate from the recommended course and run aground. No casualties. The offender suspended.

But two sheets were missing from the appendices. The numbering jumped from page forty-seven to page fifty, while the inventory listed “Diagram of lights, 2 sheets”. Lida looked at the half-page from the log that had come in the envelope. Suddenly it made her feel colder, although the saloon was heated.

At dawn the island emerged from the fog. First came a dark strip of rocks, then a white tower and a house with a blue roof. The light was off, but the lighthouse’s glass crown caught the pale sun. A man in a waterproof jacket stood on the pier. He raised his hand, and Lida recognised Ilya Korneyev at once—only his beard had turned almost white.
— I thought they’d send someone who knew how to throw papers away, he said instead of greeting her.
— I know how to read inventories.
— That’s more dangerous.

Ilya took her suitcase but left the tube of charts untouched. They went up the wooden walkway to the house. The wind pressed in from the sea, and the grass lay all one way, as though a huge brush were being drawn across the island. At the door Lida turned. Below, beyond the line of surf, the black tooth of Sukhoy Kamen showed for an instant, then vanished beneath a wave.
— Who sent the letter? she asked.
Ilya took a long time finding the right key.
— The archive, he said at last. — Sometimes old papers find their own addressee.

The lighthouse house was smaller than she remembered. The corridor where Lida had once ridden a wooden toy car could now be crossed in five steps. Photographs of ships, a barometer, and a faded evacuation plan hung on the walls. Everything else had changed: the kitchen gleamed with stainless steel, a satellite terminal stood in the radio room, and airtight frames had been fitted to the windows. Only the clock over the door was seven minutes slow—just as it had been in her grandfather’s day.

The archive occupied a room behind the workshop. Grey crates stood in rows on the floor, dated from pre-revolutionary logbooks to printouts from the latest seasons. Each carried a card: “retain”, “scan”, “dispose of”. The last pile was the tallest.
— They decided that quickly? Lida asked.
— Inspector Kruglov decided. He’ll be here in four days to sign off the automation. To him, there are two kinds of paper: what’s already in the computer, and what’s superfluous.

Ilya put the kettle on and opened the shutters. All six lights were visible from here, though by day they looked like nothing more than poles and little white houses. He named them like old acquaintances: Zapadny, Banny, Verkhny, Nizhny, Rifovy, Krestovy. Each had its own character. Rifovy flashed briefly and often; Zapadny held its light longer, as though reluctant to let a vessel go.
— And the seventh? Lida asked.
Ilya poured boiling water past the mug. He wiped the table with his palm and winced.
— Don’t start with what isn’t there. Start with the optics log for eighty-seven. If everything tallies there, you won’t need the rest.

The log turned up in a crate marked “dispose of”. Water had warped its cover, and the pages were stuck together along the spine. Lida laid them on blotting paper and began turning them with tweezers. Each evening the person on watch had recorded visibility, wind strength, and the times the lights were lit and extinguished. In the “special observations” column her grandfather had left spare phrases: “ice on south pane”, “rotation roller replaced”, “two white geese observed”.
After the October entry about the geese came three torn-out sheets.
— Two pages missing from the file, three from this, said Lida. — An odd sort of tidiness.
Ilya looked out of the window. Slanting rain lay over the sea, dividing the horizon into moving strips.
— Your grandfather wrote everything down twice. A fair copy for the authority, a rough one for himself. He used to say the sea likes its readings to have a witness.
— Where’s the rough copy?
— If I knew, the letter would have been thicker.

That was how Lida knew he had sent the envelope. She did not challenge him on it. Instead she checked the tide table on the half-sheet against the calendar for 1987. The date matched the Toros accident. Beside the lowest tide were a small circle and the letter ‘S’.

In the evening the main light came on. The electric motor set the optical apparatus gently turning, and reflections drifted across the walls. The beam returned every twelve seconds. Lida went out onto the porch. One by one the other lights answered in the darkness: distant, near, high, low. Their rhythms differed, but together they formed an order a ship’s navigator could read like a sentence.
Beyond the Rifovy light lay a black emptiness. Sukhoy Kamen should have been there.

Lida counted the flashes until her eyes began to make mistakes. On the seventh cycle she thought she saw another white point tremble low above the water. She blinked; the point was gone. Ilya stood in the doorway, holding a woollen shawl for her.
— Sometimes a wave gives the light back, he said. — Not every reflection belongs on a chart.
— But every one ought to be checked first.

That night Lida slept in her grandfather’s old room. Wind rustled behind the wallpaper, and the lens moved steadily overhead. Before bed she found seven shallow scratches on the windowsill. Six were straight; the seventh veered aside and ended in an arrow pointing out to sea.

In the morning Ilya went to check the batteries at the Nizhny light, leaving Lida the entire lighthouse for the first time. The house creaked, the pipes answered the wind, and a relay clicked from time to time in the empty radio room. She climbed the spiral staircase, counting ninety-eight steps. In childhood there had been a hundred and one. Three, apparently, had existed only because her legs were shorter.

Beneath the lantern room was a circular service room. Tool cupboards lined the walls, and a steel shaft turned at its centre. The new drive occupied half the floor, blinking green indicators. Beside it, beneath a tarpaulin, stood the old weight-driven clockwork mechanism. It was meant to go to a museum, but the word “discard” was already showing on its tag.

Lida pulled off the tarpaulin. Someone had scratched “L-7” into the brass frame. The same marking appeared on her grandfather’s sheet beside the tide table. Beneath the frame she found a narrow door painted over with the wall. The lock would not give until Lida slipped the flat end of her dividers into it. Inside were two wooden cases and a roll of sailcloth.

The first case held a spare lens sector—a heavy semicircle of glass with concentric steps. The second contained a signalling mirror panel, darkened at the edges. Three lines had been drawn in charcoal on the sailcloth, with distances marked beside them. Lida spread it out on the floor. It was a diagram of a beam: the main apparatus, the tower’s lower window, a point at sea.
The arrow ended at the letters “SK”.

She photographed the discovery and tried to call the bureau. The terminal showed a weak signal, then its screen went dark. Outside, the engine of Ilya’s launch was drawing closer. Lida had time to put the door back, but left the lens on the table.
Ilya saw it from the doorway and stopped.
— You knew, said Lida.
— I knew Semyon hadn’t thrown the glass away. I didn’t know where he’d hidden it.
— Does L-7 mean the seventh light?
Ilya went to the window and opened the lower casement. It faced away from the channel, straight towards Sukhoy Kamen. At low tide a flat slab veined with white was already visible above the water.

— It isn’t a separate light, he said. — Semyon called it the returned light. Part of the main beam went down through the spare sector. There was a panel on the rock. With everything aligned properly, the light came back out to sea in a narrow path. You could only see it from one direction.
— Why?
— The old passage between the shoals changed after every ice breakup. The official leading line took you too close to the shallows. The seventh showed an alternative channel.
— An unregistered signal. Exactly what got Grandfather dismissed.
— Exactly what saved us once.

The word “us” hung between them. Ilya closed the casement, picked up the lens case, and carried it downstairs. Lida followed, asking questions, but he spoke only of the mechanism: the fittings had rusted, the panel on the rock had been torn away, the old passage had long since silted up. Not a word about the night of the accident.
In the workshop they cleaned the glass. On one segment, a palm print remained, worked into the dust. Ilya would not let her wipe it off with alcohol.
— It’s not evidence, he said. — Just the hand of a man in a hurry.

Lida set her grandfather’s magnifying glass beside it. Through the glass, scratches in the lens became deep riverbeds. Two marks appeared on the edge of the mount: the azimuth and the downward angle. She copied them into her notebook and realised the first half of the mystery was solved. The seventh light had existed, but not where people had looked for it. It was a way of reading the water, not a point on the shore.
The second half was harder: why had a light that saved lives been named in the report as the cause of an accident?

epigraph.p: On a dry chart, the depths lie still. On a living one, they breathe.

section.p: Sukhoy Kamen could only be reached at spring low water2, when moon and sun combined their efforts and the sea withdrew farther than usual. According to the calendar, such a low tide was due at noon. Ilya checked the forecast three times and stowed a rope, a first-aid kit, and two flasks in the launch. Lida took the lens case, though he said it would be no use on the rock.

The island grew smaller as they travelled. From the water the lighthouse house looked like a white card pinned to the dark headland. The backs of granite shoals surfaced between the waves. Ilya drove the launch slowly, taking his bearings from the water’s colour rather than the navigation screen.
— Here the screen is a whole boat-length behind, he explained. — By the time the satellite tells you you’re on a rock, the propeller will have found out first.

Sukhoy Kamen proved to be not a tooth but a long slab almost entirely covered at high tide. They stepped ashore onto wet granite. Transparent seaweed lay in the pools, and shells crackled underfoot. Four bolts and the curve of a metal frame survived on the northern edge. The signalling panel was gone.

image.alt: An old tidal chart and the mark for the seventh light

section.p: Lida set up her survey board, took the coordinates, and unfolded the sailcloth diagram. The line from the lighthouse’s lower window crossed the rock exactly where the fittings were. The second line led south-east, towards a narrow passage between two shoals. On modern charts the passage was considered closed.

Meanwhile Ilya was searching the cracks for something. From one he pulled a flattened tin box. Its lid had rusted shut, but inside, beneath oiled cloth, sheets of graph paper had survived. On the first, her grandfather had drawn the shore at three stages of the tide. On the second was a profile of the seabed. The third had columns of time, wind, and depth. It was the rough log.

Some of the entries had washed away, but the margins survived. Her grandfather had written brief observations there instead of figures: “ice carried buoy away”, “Pyotr argues”, “I.K. came uninvited again”, “panel visible in fourth minute”. The initials appeared on every page.
— I.K.—is that you?
Ilya sat on the edge of the slab, watching water fill its grooves.
— I was twelve. I tagged along with my father in the launch and knew every place I wasn’t allowed to go. Semyon used to chase me out of the tower, then let me hold the survey staff.
— Why aren’t you in the report?
— Because children have no business being out at sea on a stormy night.
Lida turned the sheet over. On the back was a hurried sketch: a little launch, three figures, and a beam touching the rock. Beneath it was the date of the accident.

The tide was coming in. As they talked, they failed to notice the water cutting off their way to the launch. Ilya sprang up, grabbed the box, and told her to follow the pale vein in the granite. A wave rolled over the slab and struck Lida at the knees. The case slipped from her hands. She caught it beneath her elbow, but the notebook fell into the water.
Ilya stepped after it, and for the first time Lida saw real fear on his face—not for the notes, but of the water itself. She caught him by his jacket.
— Leave it. Those are copies.
— Not everything can be copied.

The next wave brought the notebook back to the rock. Ilya caught it with a boat hook, and they reached the launch waist-deep in icy water. By the time the engine started, Sukhoy Kamen had broken into several little black islands.
On the way back neither of them spoke. Lida held the box beneath her jacket. Rust seeped through the fabric, like the outline of an unknown continent.

They dried the sheets in the kitchen, interleaving them with napkins and old newspapers. Ilya lit the stove, but Lida’s hands still trembled. Salt dried on her skin in white specks. They could not save the whole notebook: several pages had stuck together and the ink had run. But her phone still held the morning’s photographs, and for the first time Lida was glad of her habit of photographing every stage of her work.

The rough log was more than a duplicate. Her grandfather had copied depths and times into the official tables; in the margins he had left the reasons. They told the story of a slowly changing channel. After the ice breakup of 1985, deposits had shifted the southern shoal. Large vessels could still follow the old course, but a westerly wind carried small craft towards the rocks. Her grandfather had proposed moving the leading lights. The authority had replied that a new survey was not in the plan.

So he had assembled the returned light from a spare lens and an old signalling panel. It was a temporary experiment that had no right to become permanent. Every night at low tide, Semyon switched it on for ten minutes and measured its visibility from a launch. Pyotr Korneyev, Ilya’s father, helped him.
On the last surviving sheet the entry broke off: “22 October. Wind strengthening. Toros held off Zapadny. Pyotr has gone to remove the panel. Ilya…” The rest of the paper had been torn away.
— Did Pyotr go alone? Lida asked.
Ilya laid another napkin on the table, though the sheet was already dry.

— He thought I was asleep. I hid in the bow locker. When the storm began, I came out. Father turned the launch back, but the engine choked near the southern shoal. On paper, we weren’t at sea. Otherwise he would have lost his job, and I would have lost any chance of ever coming back to the island.
— Grandfather found you?

— He saw that the portable light hadn’t come back. He switched on the lower beam. The panel was still on the rock, showing the passage. Semyon came out in the service launch, took us aboard, and left our boat in tow. That was when the Toros arrived.

The tug had been warned to keep farther west, but the captain saw the unfamiliar path of light and decided it was a new leading line. He headed straight for it from the opposite direction and ran onto the sand. The hull was undamaged. By morning the tide had floated the vessel off. A mistake without consequences, it would seem—except that the authority had found a convenient culprit.
— Grandfather could have shown them the log.

— Then he’d have had to explain who he was rescuing. Father asked him not to name us. I heard them arguing. Semyon said, “Someone else’s life isn’t worth less because it wasn’t entered on the voyage sheet.” Then he signed the report alone.

Lida looked at Ilya for a long time. For nine years she had guarded her resentment towards her grandfather, believing it the last form of loyalty left to her. Now it turned out that resentment had been built on an empty space: two missing surnames.
— You could have told me sooner.
— I could. Every year, I could. Then Father died, then Semyon. The longer you keep quiet, the more you think a confession won’t help anyone any more.
— It would have helped me.
Ilya nodded, neither making excuses nor looking away. That made it harder still for Lida to be angry.

She entered the data from the sheets in a table and overlaid her grandfather’s soundings on the modern seabed model. The figures did not match. The old alternative passage had not disappeared: it had moved almost forty metres east and grown deeper after the latest storms. Sukhoy Kamen now marked not the middle of the path but its western edge.

Lida drew a new line in red pencil. If the reflector were mounted on the surviving bolts, the returned light would lead a vessel onto a shoal. To show safe water, the panel would have to be moved to the neighbouring ledge, exposed only at the very lowest tide.
— So the seventh light is out of date too, said Ilya.
— No. Its position is out of date. They’re different things.
She smiled for the first time since her arrival. The whole of cartography rested on that difference.

title.p: The Man Who Wasn’t in the Report

section.p: Inspector Kruglov arrived a day early. A launch brought him ashore with two technicians, crates of automation equipment, and the smell of a city coffee shop. He was young, neat, and wore white trainers at the lighthouse, as though expecting the island to wipe its rocks clean for him in advance.
— Rakitina? Excellent. I hope you’ve sorted the collection already. The scanner comes tomorrow; removal is the day after.
Lida showed him the rough log, the beam diagram, and her calculations for the new passage. Kruglov listened attentively, even taking off his jacket, but his conclusion was simple:
— Historically interesting. Of no navigational use. An unregistered light creates a hazard, as the accident confirms.
— The accident confirms that the signal was seen from the wrong direction. For guiding a boat through, it worked.
— In eighty-seven. Now we have satellite correction.
— Which disappeared for forty minutes yesterday.
— That’s why there’s a backup channel.
A technician’s voice came from the radio room: the backup channel was failing its self-test. Kruglov coughed and asked them not to confuse commissioning with design decisions.

Ilya scarcely spoke over lunch. Afterwards he set a faded photograph in front of the inspector. It showed two men holding a boy wrapped in tarpaulin. Behind them the service launch gleamed white, and a thin path of light lay on the water.

— That boy is me, said Ilya. — Semyon Rakitin switched on the lower light to bring us out. The Toros ran aground later. We’re not in the report because Father went out without permission and took a child. If you need a witness, write it down.
Kruglov turned the photograph over. On the back were a date and three surnames.
— Why are you making this statement thirty-nine years later?
— Because you’re about to throw away the one piece of paper that remembers better than I do.

The inspector was silent for a long time. Then he separated the crate of rough notes from the disposal pile and put a “scan” card on it. It was less than Lida had wanted, but more than Ilya had expected.

That evening the technicians began a test changeover. They stopped the main apparatus, and the LED module took up its rhythm without a perceptible pause. The new beam was colder than the old one, with a sharper edge in the fog. Lida stood on the gallery beside Kruglov.
— Beautiful, she said.
— People usually say “soulless” at this point.
— Light isn’t obliged to have a soul. It’s obliged to be where people expect it.
Kruglov looked at her with a respect that had not been there that morning.

— Automation doesn’t put the keeper out of a job overnight, he said. — Ilya will stay for the transition season. If the archive is recognised as a site of local historical importance, the house won’t be mothballed either.
— Who has to recognise it?
— Whoever writes a convincing case for it before Monday.

Lida understood the hint. Monday was three days away. She went down to the archive, set a clean sheet before her, and began with the sentence: “The lighthouse on Cape Krestovy constitutes not a single structure, but a system of observations, decisions, and testimony.” The sentence was heavy, bureaucratic, but true. Sometimes, to save a history, you first had to translate it into the language of an inventory.

After midnight the wind shifted to the north-east. The barometer fell four divisions at once. An alarm gave a brief beep in the radio room, and a technician called for Kruglov. A storm was gathering over the island that had not been in the morning forecast.

epigraph.p: It is not the sea that needs light, but the one searching for the shore.
epigraph.text-author: An unsigned note on the back of a chart

stanza.v: As long as a window glows ashore,
the sea has a road that leads it home.
The light does not lead—it says only this:
someone is waiting right at the door.

poem.text-author: An unsigned note on the back of a chart

section.p: The storm came not as a wall but as the vanishing of distances. First the far shore disappeared, then the Rifovy light, then the water beneath the windows. Fog mingled with rain, and the lighthouse beam struck a white emptiness. The wind battered the tower in short, heavy blows.

At twenty-two forty-seven the satellite channel broke off. A minute later the backup radio fell silent: lightning had taken out the antenna on Cape Zapadny. The technicians switched the power to batteries. The new module kept flashing to within a tenth of a second, but no one beyond the island answered.

Ilya brought a paper list of vessels received before the connection failed. In the area were the cargo ship Polyarnik, a fishing trawler, and the small research launch Kayra, with six people aboard. The first two had managed to confirm a northerly course. The Kayra should have passed through the southern channel an hour earlier.
— She draws a metre and a half, said Ilya. — In normal water that’s enough. With this wind she’ll be driven towards the old passage.

Kruglov demanded that the emergency transmitter be started. The technician showed him a burnt connector. They could raise a portable antenna to the gallery, but lightning was striking too close. All that remained was the sound signal, useless against the sea’s roar, and the light.
— The main light marks the designated channel, said Kruglov. — They ought to keep to it.

Lida spread her grandfather’s soundings and the fresh chart on the floor. The north-easterly wind was driving water out of the bay. The level was falling faster than the tide table predicted. The designated channel was growing shallow, but the eastern branch by Sukhoy Kamen would remain open for another hour.
— If the Kayra has lost her engine or her bearings, the current is carrying her here. The main light will stay hidden by the fog. They need the lower beam.
— Unregistered and untested, Kruglov snapped.
— Tested thirty-nine years ago, said Ilya.
— The shore has shifted since then, Lida added. — That’s why we can’t use the old panel. But we’ve calculated a new direction.

She pointed to the red line. To reflect it back from the rock, they needed a reflector on the eastern ledge. Putting one there now was impossible. Ilya suggested directing the beam at the white wall of an abandoned fish warehouse across the bay. From there the light would fall almost along the safe channel, but its reflection would be broad and weak.
— We don’t have to guide them all the way, said Lida. — It’s enough to show them which side of the shoal to pass.
Kruglov looked at the chart, then at the clock. The decision contradicted the instructions; doing nothing contradicted the purpose of the instructions themselves.
— We record every action, he said. — We switch on the lower beam only after sighting the vessel. Ten minutes. We leave the main operating mode unchanged.

Ilya was already carrying the lens case upstairs. The electric light on the staircase went out. The tower shuddered, the motor above stopped, and for the first time in many years the main Krestovy light went dark.

The backup generator would not start. Sea foam had been driven into its air intake, and a sensor had cut off the fuel supply. The technicians worked below while Ilya and Lida climbed to the lantern, lighting the steps with headlamps. Kruglov carried the action log and entered the time every thirty seconds.

Without its rotation, the lens looked like a vast, transparent animal. The beam from a handheld emergency lamp splintered in its facets and scattered across the walls. Ilya opened the cabinet of the old drive. The weights were still there, the chain greased. To start the mechanism, they had to raise three cast-iron weights the height of the tower.

They turned the winch together. The metal resisted, and their palms slipped. On the sixth turn Lida felt the weight below cease to be motionless. On the twelfth the old mechanism sighed. Ilya released the brake, and the lens began to move slowly around the lamp.
The technicians powered the LED module directly from the battery trolley. A white beam struck into the fog. Not as bright as usual, but steady. The main light had returned.

Now they had to assemble the lower one. They fitted the spare sector into slots by the service-room window. The mountings did not match the new frame; Kruglov took off his belt, and Ilya added copper wire. Lida set the angle by her grandfather’s marks, then corrected it for the passage’s shift. With every minute the water level changed.

image.alt: A night storm and the seventh beam above the water

section.p: At twenty-three twenty-eight a sound came through the fog—not a horn, but the uneven thud of an engine. Ilya switched off his headlamp and pressed close to the glass. A red sidelight flashed low over the water. Vanished. Appeared again, farther to the left.
— Kayra, he said. — She’s coming sideways.

Lida opened the lower casement. Wind burst into the room, scattering the sheets of the log. They secured the mirror panel outside, and part of the main light went downwards. At first the beam sank into the water just off the shore. Lida raised the sector by one division. A white strip touched the warehouse wall, and the wall answered with a dim rectangle.
A path appeared on the water—not smooth, but broken by waves into hundreds of short lights. It ran east of Sukhoy Kamen, exactly where Lida had drawn the red line.
The launch did not change course.
— They might take it for a reflection, said Kruglov.

Ilya covered the panel with his palm, uncovered it, covered it again: three short, three long, three short. Then he indicated the direction with two long flashes. The Kayra answered with her running lights. The red point began moving to the right.

Below, the technicians got the generator working again. The main beam blazed at full strength, and for a second the lower path became dazzlingly white. Lida saw the whole launch: raised bow, people by the wheelhouse, torn canopy. Sukhoy Kamen lay black astern. Less than two hundred metres separated them.
— Farther right, she whispered, though they could not hear her. — Keep the light to port.

The launch crossed the reflected beam, then came back to it at the right angle. The engine’s beat grew steadier. Five minutes later the Kayra disappeared behind the eastern breakwater, into sheltered water. Word came from the radio room: the portable radio link had come back to life, and the crew confirmed six people aboard and damage to the steering gear. No one was hurt.

Kruglov recorded the time the lower light was switched off. Ilya released the brake of the old drive, allowing the weights to bring the lens slowly to a halt, but the new motor had already taken up the rotation. The tower was working like a modern lighthouse again. Only a wet chart lay on the floor, and a pale strip still reached from the lower window.
Lida removed the spare sector. On the glass, beside the old palm print, a new one remained—her own. She did not wipe it away.

In the morning the sea looked guilty. The wind had dropped, the clouds had lifted, and clean water gleamed on the rocks. The Kayra lay by the breakwater with her steering cable patched up. Her captain, a short woman in a red hat, brought a bag of coffee to the lighthouse and demanded to see whoever had thought up the flashing wall.

— We lost contact by the Rifovy shoal, she told them. — The navigation display kept jumping, and we couldn’t see the main leading lights. Then a white dotted line appeared on the water. At first we thought we were imagining it. When the light flashed the distress signal, we realised: the shore was talking to us.

Kruglov documented the night’s use of the light as an emergency visual aid. The wording did not mention the seventh light, but her grandfather’s diagram, the new soundings, and the photograph from 1987 were attached to the report. Ilya signed his testimony with his full name. Lida put her signature beside his.

The Toros file could not be overturned with a single document, but it could be supplemented. The bureau requested the original logbooks and suspended disposal of the archive. The district administration agreed to consider the lighthouse house as a historical station. Even the old clockwork drive received a new card: “retain as part of the site”.

For two days Lida worked on the shore. She set up survey staffs, took check soundings from the Kayra, and gathered tide data. On the new chart the southern branch curved like a thin blue ribbon. It was not a recommended channel and might never become one. But now its existence had been measured, signed, and dated.

She marked the seventh light as a historical emergency method of finding one’s way, rather than a permanent navigational aid. Beside it she placed a warning: the reflector’s position must be recalculated after every ice season. The chart honestly said not only where to go, but how much it could be trusted.

cite.p: Precision is not the absence of doubt. It is the boundary of what is known, correctly marked.

section.p: Before she left, Ilya brought her a small wooden box. Inside were her grandfather’s pencils, a folding ruler, and a compass with cracked glass.
— Semyon left this with me after the inquiry. Told me to give it to you when you began drawing your own shores instead of correcting other people’s.
— Why didn’t you give it to me sooner?
— You’d have asked how I came by it. And back then I hadn’t learned how to answer.

Lida opened the compass. Its needle trembled, but stubbornly returned to north. On the inside of the lid her grandfather had scratched the same four numbers that were on the envelope. No secret code, no last will—just the coordinates of a place where a mistake made and a life saved had turned out to be one story.

The motor vessel sailed at noon. Ilya stood on the pier, Kruglov argued with the technicians about the antenna fittings, and the Kayra’s captain waved her red hat. The lighthouse grew smaller but stayed in sight longer than the island. Even by day its glass returned the sunlight from time to time.

Lida spread a clean sheet on the little table and drew the first line of a new shore. She was neither copying her grandfather’s line nor tracing a satellite image, but joining her own soundings. The line came out uneven. She could have smoothed it, but left it as it was. The sea was under no obligation to match a beautiful drawing.
In the lower corner Lida wrote: “As of September 2026.” Then she added the surnames of Ilya, the Kayra’s captain, and both technicians. Every chart ought to have witnesses.

In spring Lida returned to Tonky. Ice still held in the bays, but open water was already moving over Sukhoy Kamen. A blue plaque had appeared on the door of the lighthouse house: “Navigation Station and Archive of Northern Routes”. They had decided against the word “museum”: inside the house people still worked, argued, and dried wet charts.

The main light ran automatically. Ilya stayed on as keeper for the transition season, teaching the young technicians to listen to the motor before looking at its indicator. Kruglov sent a glass display case for the old lens, but the sector had not yet been put in it: it was taking part in trials of the emergency system.

They made the new reflector foldable and kept it ashore. It could be set up only on the decision of the watchkeeper and at precise coordinates. At last the seventh light had instructions, a number, and a place in the register. It was no less mysterious for that—only now someone answered for the mystery.

Lida climbed to the room beneath the lens. A logbook lay on the table, open at its first clean page. She entered the visibility, wind, and water level, then added in the “special observations” column: “Two white geese observed above the cape.”
Then she opened the lower window. There was not a single vessel at sea in need of help. The main beam had not yet been lit. The white daylight lay calm and even on the water.
Lida checked the direction all the same.
Leading lights are installed in pairs at different heights. When a navigator sees them aligned vertically, the vessel is on the prescribed line of a safe course.
Spring low water is part of the particularly strong tidal cycle at new and full moon, when the Moon’s and the Sun’s gravitational forces act along the same line.
